articles.title: Israel’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalition
articles.summary: Incumbent could turn defeat into another term in office as rival parties erect confected barrier to unseating him
body: Hours before the final results from Israel’s elections were in, several things were clear. Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition had lost its mandate, and the opposition had a firm majority.

But most of Israel’s Jewish opposition ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties, in the course of a racist election campaign that saw Netanyahu painting Palestinian citizens as an enemy inside the state.

The self-imposed ban on a broader opposition alliance, if it holds, offers Netanyahu the prospect of turning his defeat into another term in office – or at least a prolonged mandate as caretaker prime minister and perhaps another round of elections.

This confected barrier to unseating Netanyahu became the focus of Israeli media and analysts. “No Clear Government” announced the newspaper Israel Hayom. “Road to Unity Government Has Been Paved”, read an article on Channel 12.

Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, attacked that framing. “Netanyahu lost. I know how to count,” he said in a statement calling for a government with Palestinians, who make up about 20% of Israel’s population.

“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said. “We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Arab citizens of Israel.”

Other Israelis were even more direct. “If you stop being racist two amazing things will happen to you,” musician Yali Sobol wrote in a Facebook post. “First, you will stop being racist. Second, you will discover you have won.”
While Palestinian-led parties do not describe themselves as Zionist, neither do some of the ultra-orthodox groups who are a key part of Netanyahu’s current coalition.

A survey taken as polls closed on election day showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with the Palestinian-led Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu, political psychology researcher Eran Halperin said.
But opposition leaders were silent on Wednesday, as they apparently tried to balance their desire to unseat Netanyahu with promises against working with Palestinians.

Former general Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the biggest opposition party, has not directly ruled out governing with Palestinians but laid out conditions that made it politically impossible for them to join a coalition.

Palestinians have been clearer about their priorities. “We are ready and prepared to pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government,” Yousef Jabareen, leader of the larger Joint List, said on Wednesday. “The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership.”
The Islamist Ra’am party put a Jewish former police chief in second position on their slate, in a signal of their commitment to working with Jewish Israelis.

A precedent from three decades ago, when Yitzhak Rabin relied on Palestinian support for a minority government as he sought a negotiated end to the Israel-Palestine conflict, gets little mention in contemporary Israeli political debate.
Netanyahu put racism at the heart of his campaign, in a strategy critics said was designed both to bolster voter support and complicate post-election coalition negotiations for the opposition.
A slogan featured on many of his election posters, “The right or Palestine”, framed 20% of the population as an enemy within Israel’s borders.
Related: A bitter night in Israel for all who craved a fresh start. Netanyahu survives for now – and we are more divided than ever | Dahlia Scheindlin

On election night he shrugged off the loss of around 10 seats from the 64 seat-coalition he assembled in 2022 – a severe rebuke from voters by most counts – to claim that his vision for Israel had been vindicated in the poll.

The Knesset overall has shifted further right, as have young Israelis, and after the results came in, he issued an open invitation to put their opposition to Palestinian parties ahead of their opposition to him.
“The rightwing bloc has a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public,” he said. “We must form a strong national-right government”.

Many in Israel described this election as existential, as they struggled to halt the erosion of democracy inside Israel’s pre-1967 borders, and secure a State Commission of Inquiry into the 7 October attacks.

For Palestinian citizens facing surging crime, discrimination and home demolitions inside Israel and watching family and friends endure ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank and a war of annihilation in Gaza, that was viscerally true, and they came out in record numbers.

Israel describes itself as a Jewish and democratic state. If the representatives of Palestinians are now effectively excluded from government because of their race, Netanyahu will have turned that promise into more of a choice – between a Jewish future or a democratic one.

articles.title: Putin hails Elon Musk’s ‘genius’ amid plans for Russian version of Starlink
articles.summary: Russia plans to build own version of US billionaire’s satellite communications to help attack Ukraine
body: Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s genius and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine.

The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk’s SpaceX with Russia’s gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation.

“Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Russian leader said, according to the Tass news agency. “How many of these [satellites] does he have in orbit? More than 5,000, and we’re only taking the first steps.”

The true number of active SpaceX satellites is estimated at about 10,000, which provide the high-speed internet service that has been the subject of a diplomatic row between Musk, the US and Ukraine earlier this month.

A military version of Starlink, called Starshield, was suddenly restricted one night in the middle of October, preventing Ukraine from conducting medium drone attacks and hampering some of its anti-drone air defences.

Initially, Musk, an ally of the US president, Donald Trump, denied that he had ordered a throttling of the internet connection, before saying at the end of last week that he had closed a loophole in which the civilian Starlink had been used by the military.

Putin appeared to be trying to flatter Musk, whose control of the communications technology has raised questions about the US billionaire’s leverage over the White House and the impact he is able to have on Ukraine’s war effort.

“We are in close contact with our American partners – including Mr Musk – because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and ​to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin said.

Starlink does not work in Russia and its use by Russia inside Ukraine was restricted earlier this year. Meanwhile, Moscow has begun to develop an alternative system, though, with an estimated 26 working satellites, its capacity is limited.

Last week, after about 10 days of restriction, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, announced that “Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored” and that the speeds were “now where they need to be”.

Few believe the issue is permanently settled, with relations between Zelenskyy and Trump fraught in the run-up to the US midterm elections next Tuesday. Trump has also reached out to Putin, agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow early in October in an effort to reduce the oil price before Americans go to the polls.

Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he hoped proposed trilateral peace talks, involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, would take place between 6 and 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE, shortly after the midterms.

“We are waiting for the American side. I think that they’ll be ready with all the answers after the elections,” the Ukrainian leader said at a press conference in The Hague with the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten.

Earlier, Zelenskyy said he had spoken to Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, as it emerged that Britain would provide £10bn in extra financing for Ukraine over the next three years – and an immediate £500m for air defence systems.

The additional aid was, Zelenskyy said, “a truly strong and very timely step” that came “as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone” as the war heads towards what is expected to be its most difficult winter yet.

John Healey, the UK chancellor, announced the extra funding as part of the government’s annual budget. “The prime minister and I called President Zelenskyy to tell him about our commitments in the budget today. He told us: ‘You’ve made my day’.”

The Dutch government also said it would provide €500m in military support for the winter, and a further €1.2bn in non-military aid, partly to help fund urgent repairs to Ukraine’s utilities and manufacturing.
Kyiv has been relentlessly attacked by Moscow this autumn as Russian forces fail to make progress on the frontlines in the east of Ukraine.

Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since the middle of October, Zelenskyy said overnight, hitting power plants and other key targets in an effort to cause a humanitarian crisis in the capital.

articles.title: ‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of Spain’s second deadly train crash in 10 months
articles.summary: Passengers describe carriages full of seriously injured people after crash that has claimed at least 68 lives
body: Josimar Medina woke a little before 9am on Wednesday to find himself airborne and hurtling through his carriage on the fast train from Madrid to Seville.
“I remember flying through the air and looking for my girlfriend, who was also shooting through the air,” said Medina, a 37-year-old tourist from the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo.
Once he landed, he looked around and realised just how lucky he and his girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, had been.

“I saw people with cuts, people covered in blood, people missing limbs, and I saw one person who had nothing left below the chest,” said Medina. “I saw people with their heads crushed and people with mutilated arms.”

The Peruvian stood recounting the details of Wednesday’s deadly rail crash, in which at least 68 people were killed and dozens more were injured, wearing a light brown T-shirt stained with the blood of a young American man he had helped move to safety.

Medina and Maia had been in the seventh carriage of the state-operated Renfe train that smashed into the back of a train run by the private Iryo company on the same line from the capital to the south of Spain. Had they been any further forward, they could well have been among the accident’s fatalities.

As it was, the couple climbed out of the train and helped the injured while they waited for medics and Guardia Civil officers to arrive at the scene of the crash, which took place amid vineyards and olive groves near the small town of Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, near the city of Toledo.

Within hours of the crash, Urda had been transformed into a frantic emergency response centre, with a local sports centre pressed into service as a triage post for the walking wounded. Cars, vans and trucks from the emergency services in Castilla-La Mancha and neighbouring Madrid crowded the streets.
Fredrich and Arabella Barilea, a couple from the Philippines who now live in Dubai, were on the Iryo train, and Fredrich was sent flying by the impact.

“One guy was shouting, ‘Get out! Get out! Another train could hit!” said Fredrich. “We saw all the people were also getting off. Many of them had head injuries and were covered in blood. We just got as far away from the train as we could.”
Eventually, buses arrived to ferry the lightly injured survivors to Urda – although the Barileas said they were too shocked and confused to know where exactly they had been brought.

“It all happened in a split second,” said Arabella. “The table we were sitting at just disappeared in the crash. I feel like we’re on our second life. You never know what could happen. We’re very grateful.”

Around the couple, people queued patiently on the street as they waited to board coaches. Wearing torn and bloodstained clothes and, in some cases, bandages on their heads, they stared, mute and uncomprehending. Spain may have been in mourning, as the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said during his visit to Urda, but many of those fortunate enough to survive Spain’s second fatal rail crash in less than a year were still too deep in shock to begin grieving.

Ata Yelkaya, a young tourist from Turkey, usually takes the bus when he travels around Spain. On Wednesday, however, he had decided to try the Iryo. Sleepy and assuming his train had come to a halt at a station, he had switched off his tablet and pulled up his hood in preparation for a nap. At 8.53am, he felt what he would later learn was the impact of the Renfe train smashing into the carriages behind him.

“I woke up with a bump and hit my head on the seat in front of me,” he said, “I looked across at an elderly couple near me and saw that the woman had a cut in her eyebrow. That’s when I knew something serious had happened.”
When he looked out of the window, he saw the carriages behind his – carriage No 5 – had come off the track and that many people had been killed or injured.

“Everyone was in shock but I tried to help other people get off the train,” he said. “I’m from Turkey and I lived through the 2023 earthquake there, so I stayed calm and tried to think about what to do and how to get out. It was only when I got out and saw some of the dead people that it hit me. I think everyone was in shock; too shocked even to panic or to scream.”

Wednesday’s disaster stirs memories of the Adamuz rail crash in January, in which 46 people died. Once again, a small town has found itself at the centre of a national disaster and, once again, local people have rallied to help, bringing food and water to a hall that had been set up as a centre for those searching for their relatives.

But, as also happened at Adamuz, the solidarity and kindness on display is likely to turn to anger over the coming hours as people seek answers as to how one of Europe’s most modern and extensive high-speed rail networks could experience two deadly accidents that have between them claimed at least 114 lives in the space of just 10 months. With a snap general election just a month away, many voters could use their votes to register their fury over another rail disaster. The “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash – as Spain’s transport minister has called them – will need to be explained as swiftly thoroughly as possible.

For all the rush to action and unity on display, there was also a sickening sense of deja vu. One woman from Urda, who had spent the morning driving people to town from the crash site, had few words to describe what she had seen and heard.
“Mejor no verlo,” she said – “it’s better not to see something like this”. Again.

articles.title: Coalition talks loom in Israel as Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs set to fall short of majority
articles.summary: Projections show votes for Palestinian parties surged in a tight contest that saw the highest turnout in decades
body: Israel’s future hung in the balance on Wednesday as it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu had lost his governing majority, and his political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s elections.

The leader of the Jewish opposition bloc, the retired general Gadi Eisenkot, appeared to rule out such a broad coalition in a premature declaration of victory overnight for what he called a “Zionist majority”.

As the vote count proceeded on Wednesday, initial exit poll projections that Eisenkot’s bloc would have a narrow lead over Netanyahu’s coalition looked increasingly in doubt as the prime minister’s bloc edged ahead, with the votes of deployed soldiers and other absentee ballots (about 14% of the total electorate) yet to be fully counted.

With the remaining 86% of the votes tallied, both Jewish blocs looked certain to fall short of the 61 Knesset seats needed for a majority government, leaving Eisenkot and his allies facing a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 16-19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.

Donald Trump took credit for Netanyahu’s better than expected performance so far, claiming his overt backing in the run-up to the vote had made the difference. “When the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot,” Trump said, adding that the result appeared to be heading for a stalemate or a Netanyahu win.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s Change bloc, urged Eisenkot to negotiate with the two Palestinian parties, the Joint List and Ra’am (the United Arab List).

“We have no future here if we don’t stop being afraid. And if we don’t put an end to racism. We can no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist distinction between Jewish and Arab votes,” Golan said in a post on X.
Related: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape

“Anyone who tries to erase the votes of Arab citizens is surrendering to Netanyahu and giving up on Israel,” he added, pointing out that Netanyahu relied on ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties that were non-Zionist and opposed conscription for their constituents.

Noa Landau, a commenter writing in Haaretz, argued that by making Zionism the test for forming a coalition, excluding potential partners, while the prime minister had not, Eisenkot had fallen “into the trap Netanyahu laid for him over the course of the election campaign”.

The Joint List leader, Yousef Jabareen, said its strong performance meant it “can’t be ignored under any political scenario”. He said Netanyahu’s government, especially its extremist national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, “has made life bitter for every Arab citizen”.

“We will be ready to pave the way to oust the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich – and send them home,” Jabareen said. Another Joint List official described the choice facing the Jewish opposition as “supremacy or building democracy”.

Counting all the votes could take another few days, with absentee ballots the last to be tallied. Most of those are from deployed soldiers. The army vote usually swings right, but that broad picture may be complicated by the fact that a lot of older, more moderate reservists are now on active duty.

Once all the votes are accounted for, it will be up to Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, to give one of the party leaders six weeks to form a government. If the first choice fails, the opportunity passes to his rival. In the weeks of political wrangling likely to ensue, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot are expected to lure defectors from each other’s camps.

Netanyahu would remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new majority is formed. He might expect to benefit if the deadlock leads to another round of elections. Tens of thousands of diaspora Israelis who returned to vote on Tuesday, and were mostly opposed to the governing coalition, might not return for another vote, for example.

The Palestinian parties and Jewish centre-left have been urging the opposition to focus on finding common cause in the Knesset, replacing the speaker and pursuing legislation that the factions can agree on, such as ordering an independent review into the security failures that led to the 7 October attack by Hamas in 2023.
On Wednesday, Herzog urged all parties to keep an “open mind” in trying to build a new government coalition.
“We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” he said.

The election happened in the midst of Israel’s war in Gaza – barely mentioned in the course of the campaign, despite the fact that Israel has been accused of committing genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and Netanyahu is wanted by the international criminal court for alleged war crimes.

A UN commission of human rights experts reported on Monday that Israel had continued to commit genocidal acts against Palestinian civilians in Gaza after a ceasefire was declared in October 2025. Since then 1,431 Palestinians have been killed by the Israeli military, including 300 children.

The report, by the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said: “Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”

Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Daniel Meron, rejected the report as an “attempt to destroy the Jewish state” and “to undermine Israel’s ​legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend itself”.

Eisenkot and much of his bloc support the war in Gaza, and sought to make the election a referendum on Netanyahu. The turnout was nearly 78%, the highest since 1999, with marked increases in the number of serving military members voting.
Political deadlock has led to repeated votes in the past. Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections.

Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, governing for 19 of the past 30 years, and its most tenacious political survivor. Entangled in a long-running corruption trial, he and his far-right coalition had stoked xenophobic fears and suggested Israel would be vulnerable to a nuclear attack without him.
The campaign, febrile even by Israeli standards, included Netanyahu posting a picture of a nuclear explosion devastating Tel Aviv on the eve of the polls opening.

Since the deadly attack launched by Hamas on Israel’s southern communities on 7 October 2023, Israel has devastated Gaza and killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, fought Hezbollah in Lebanon, occupied new territory in Syria and launched a war with the US against Iran.

articles.title: Derrick Harriott obituary
articles.summary: Singer, songwriter, producer and record label owner who was a leading figure in Jamaican pop music
body: Derrick Harriott, who has died aged 87 following a long illness, was an influential figure in Jamaican popular music.
A singer-songwriter who began his career in 1958 leading the pioneering harmony group the Jiving Juniors, Harriott had an intrinsic feel for music and an ease with tackling diverse styles.
His distinctive productions helped artists such as Keith and Tex, the Kingstonians and Junior Murvin to come to prominence in the late 1960s, and the Ethiopians, Big Youth and Scotty in the 70s.

An early mentor to Dennis Brown, Harriott was also one of the first to collaborate with King Tubby, commissioning the experimental engineer to mix the captivating dub B-sides to singles such as Brown’s Concentration and the Crystalites’ Blacula in 1973.

The youngest of six children, of whom a sister died in infancy, Harriott spent his formative years in a staunch Seventh-day Adventist household on Duke Street in downtown Kingston. His parents both worked at the nearby Excelsior College, where Harriott’s uncle, Wesley Arthur Powell, was headteacher, and after his mother emigrated to New York, Harriott’s father ran a small commercial school.

Music was an important part of daily life, since his father was a clarinettist, his uncle, Samuel Powell, a singer and his brother, Winston, a professional saxophonist. He discovered jazz balladeers such as Billy Eckstine and Nat King Cole, doo-wop harmony group the Ink Spots and local spiritual singer Jimmy Tucker through radio broadcasts, all of which influenced his approach to singing, as did Donnie Elbert’s forlorn ballad What Can I Do, which he heard on a local sound system.

While attending Excelsior in 1957, Harriott entered a talent contest held by the journalist Vere Johns at the Palace theatre with a rendition of the Turbans’ When You Dance, and subsequently formed the duo Sang and Harriott with fellow Excelsior student Claude Sang Jr, whose brother, Herman, led a popular session band, the City Slickers.

Sang and Harriott won a series of talent contests with original ballad You’re Mine, All Mine, and after Sang moved to New York to further his education, Harriott formed the Jiving Juniors with fellow Excelsior student Eugene Dwyer and Dwyer’s friend, Maurice Wynter, with Herman Sang joining on the piano.

In August 1959, Harriott joined his mother in New York but frequently returned to Jamaica to record and perform with the Jiving Juniors. The group’s Lollipop Girl was the breakthrough hit recorded for Duke Reid in 1960 and the spiritual Over the River was a big hit for Clement Dodd in 1961; recordings were also made for Chris Blackwell.

Back in New York in 1962, Harriott formed a new Jiving Juniors with Claude Sang, Valmont Burke, and Winston Service of the Downbeats. Sessions with the Teacho Wiltshire Orchestra yielded the hit Sugar Dandy, which Harriott produced and issued on the newly formed Crystal label.

Harriott then launched his solo career with his popular cover of What Can I Do, which, like Sugar Dandy, was delivered in a convincing falsetto, his ability to switch between tenor and the higher register giving Harriott an edge on his rivals.

The wide range enabled Harriott to subsequently broaden his repertoire, his solo successes of the mid-60s including the mento John Tom, the soul ballad I’m Only Human and edgy rock-steady tearjerker Walk the Streets, as well as the Murvin-penned biblical allegory, Solomon. But Harriott will always be best remembered for The Loser, a 1967 landmark recounting romantic missteps that was expertly arranged by bassist Boris Gardiner, the song framed by Joe Isaacs’ offbeat drum rolls and Lloyd Delprat’s choppy piano chords.

Soon after, Harriott opened Derrick’s One Stop, a record shop on King Street in Kingston. Focusing more on record production, he scored with Rudy Mills’ John Jones, a tale of romantic betrayal that was popular with skinhead audiences in Britain, as was the Kingstonians’ Sufferer; Keith and Tex’s adaptation of the Temptations’ Don’t Look Back and the Spanishtonians’ Stop That Train were also successful, as was the Ethiopians’ Rastafari-themed No Baptism.

Scotty’s Riddle I This was a chart topper in 1971 and his Draw Your Brakes appeared on the soundtrack of The Harder They Come; Big Youth’s Cool Breeze charted in 1973, just as Harriott moved his shop to larger premises at Twin Gates Plaza in the Half Way Tree business district.

During the 70s and 80s, Harriott’s greatest solo successes came through adaptations of soul, funk and disco: Psychedelic Train was partly inspired by the Temptations’ Psychedelic Shack and there were hit adaptations of the Chi-Lites’ weepy ballad Have You Seen Her?, Ronnie Jones’ funky disco foray Soul Sister and Don Covay’s jealousy track Checkin’ Out, as well as the sensual soul-influenced original Skin to Skin and a funky reggae adaptation of Dazz Band’s futuristic disco-funk track, Let It Whip.

Although his output waned from the mid-80s, Harriott continued to perform to audiences internationally, his appearances at the Legends of Ska festival in Toronto in 2002 and at the London International Ska festival in 2015 among the most memorable.
He was awarded the Order of Distinction in 2009 for his services to the Jamaican Music Industry and a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Jamaica Reggae Industry Association in 2019.
Harriott is survived by his eight children, his sister, Loy Shegog, and numerous grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
• Derrick Clifton Harriott, singer, songwriter and record producer, born 6 February 1939; died 24 October 2026

articles.title: Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network
articles.summary: Questions were raised before Toledo crash over rail safety in a country where train travel has surged by 40%
body: Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe and the second largest in the world after China, has long been a point of pride in the country. But Wednesday’s deadly crash – the second in nine months – has recast the spotlight on questions about safety.

Officials said at least 68 people were killed on Wednesday morning after a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks, leading to the derailment of several carriages. The two trains were believed to be carrying 544 passengers.

Speaking to reporters, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, traced the collision back to a security system that had stopped working at about 8.30am local time. The computer malfunction brought an estimated six trains to a halt along a 63km stretch of track.

Soon after, the central command in Madrid instructed one of the trains involved in the crash to resume service at normal speeds, sending it colliding into a train that was still sitting stationary on the tracks, said Puente. “It was the control centre – via its operators – that made the decision to resume operations, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he added.
State-owned rail operator Renfe said in a statement that its train had been instructed to continue on its way and had crashed into ​the stationary Iryo train “for reasons we don’t know”.
The accident follows a crash in January that killed 46 people and left dozens more injured near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.

Media on Wednesday were swift to point to the parallels between the two crashes: both involved the same train operators and took place on the line connecting Madrid to the southern region of Andalusia, which is the oldest on Spain’s high-speed network.
The first crash sparked conversation over safety on the line, a debate that rail unions say has continued.

Wednesday’s disaster came a day before a planned 24-hour work stoppage at Renfe by Spain’s largest train drivers union. “Our goal is to change the system and make it safer,” the union said earlier this month.

Their reasons for taking action ranged from the need for climate emergency protocols to ensuring channels of communication for workers to convey concerns. The union also called for guarantees that trains would be “reliable and safe”, adding: “We demand real and definitive technical solutions to the safety and reliability issues that have long plagued our rolling stock.”
It has also called a rolling, six-day strike for drivers at the high-speed rail operator Ouigo.

The January crash sparked a bout of political finger-pointing over whether Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party government had spent enough on railway maintenance in a country where travel by train accounts for about 57% of all transport.

While the causes of the January crash remain under investigation, a preliminary report suggested that it could have been the result of defects in the track or in a weld between two sections of track. The report noted, however, that several other possibilities were also being investigated.

Train travel grew by 40% from 2019 to 2024, coinciding with a period in which the country opened up its rail network to private companies. In the first half of this year, 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain.
The government says it has increased spending on railway network maintenance by 54% since taking power in 2018.

Spain spends more than any other country on its high-speed network, averaging about €1.5bn (£1.26bn) a year from 2018 to 2022, according to a Reuters analysis of EU data. More than 90% of Spain’s train network is equipped with the highest level of safety control systems in the EU.
Much of the funding, however, has seemingly been directed at new infrastructure, with about 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades.

Data from the European Commission suggests Spain’s maintenance investment in its 4,000km (2,500 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged behind countries such as Germany or Switzerland although some of this could be attributed to differences in the age of the rail lines and the cost of public works and materials.

Until this year, Spain had among the lowest accident rates in the EU, with just one or fewer fatalities per thousand kilometres of track, according to data from Eurostat, the statistics arm of the EU.

On Wednesday, Spain’s prime minister said measures would be taken to rebuild trust in the country’s high-speed rail system. “Because it is simply unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year, as we have,” said Sánchez.
The crash was Spain’s worst rail accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the north-western city of Santiago de Compostela.

articles.title: Spain’s Sánchez declares three days of mourning after at least 68 killed in Toledo train crash
articles.summary: High-speed service travelling from Madrid to Seville ran into back of another, knocking two carriages off track
body: The Spanish prime minister has declared three days of mourning after at least 68 people were killed and dozens more injured in a collision between two high-speed trains in central Spain.

The trains were travelling in the same direction on the line that stretches from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to Seville on Wednesday when one of the trains ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking several carriages off the track.

The tragedy marked the second deadly train accident this year in Spain. “All of Spain is in mourning,” the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said from the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha. It was “unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in the same year, as we have”, he said.

Footage broadcast by the regional channel CMM TV ​showed a derailed train with at least one carriage remaining on an elevated section of track. Twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the line.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, said such rear-end collisions were “highly unlikely” as he suggested that the accident may have been caused by human error made in “inexplicable” circumstances.

He said the LZB signalling system, which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied, had gone down at about 8.30am local time due to a computer malfunction. As a result, an estimated six trains had been halted along a stretch of around 63km, he said.

The task of monitoring the rail lines then fell to a 24-hour command centre in Madrid. The centre instructed at least two of the trains to continue as normal, despite the fact that there was still a “stop signal” in place on the line, said Puente.

“It was the control centre, through its operators, that made the decision to resume traffic, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he said. “Clearly, it was a wrong decision … I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts.”

The Castilla-La Mancha regional government said on Wednesday afternoon that the death toll had risen to 68 as rescue ​teams continued to ⁠search ​through the wreckage ​of ​the derailed ​carriages. Castilla-La Mancha’s leader, Emiliano García-Page, told reporters that more victims were likely as “it has not yet been possible to reach the bottom of the carriages”.
Another 73 people needed medical treatment in hospital, he said, including 15 who were in serious condition.

Miguel, ‌a passenger travelling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains, described the moment of the accident to Cope radio. “We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were ‌about to derail,” he said. “Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train – I imagine it must have been ​the other one.”

The transport minister on Wednesday confirmed that the collision involved a train from Spain’s state-owned Renfe company and the private rail company Iryo – the same two companies whose trains were also involved in a crash in Adamuz in January in which 46 people were killed.

In Wednesday’s disaster, the Iryo train was travelling ahead on the tracks and had been sitting stationary when the Renfe train was told by the control centre to resume its journey. The Renfe train then travelled approximately 25km before colliding with the Iryo train about 17 minutes later.
The speed at which the Renfe train was travelling remains unknown, the transport minister told reporters, though the section of rail on which it was travelling allows for speeds of up to 200km/hour.

Puente said that similar erroneous instructions had been given to at least one other train on Wednesday morning. “And it was the engineer of one of the trains who corrected the command centre and told them he can’t resume normal operation – it has to be [an] on-sight operation,” Puente said, citing a protocol that allows trains to advance but at a greatly reduced speed in order to ensure that there are not other trains sitting on the tracks ahead. “The operator said: ‘OK, on-sight operation.’”

Sánchez said the causes of the accident were under investigation. If it emerged that it was due to failures in the security system or negligence, these shortcomings would be addressed with the “utmost severity”, he added.

“Everything strongly suggests that the causes of the two accidents [Wednesday’s and January’s] are completely unrelated, but it is not up to me to say so,” he said. “But what is clear is that, if we need – as we certainly do – to further strengthen safety in order to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail system, it will be done.”
Manuel Galán, the mayor ​of ​Urda near the city of Toledo, said he had ​been ‌asked by ​emergency ​services to prepare a sports hall to accommodate the injured.
Spain’s main political parties, which are gearing up for next month’s general election, suspended their planned activities for the day.

The opposition People’s party leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said on X: “Very concerned about the information we are getting about a new rail accident. The priority now is to attend to the victims and support their families. My full support to the emergency teams working on the ground.”
Spain’s football federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled for Wednesday.
Reuters and Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title: In Serbia, a new type of democracy is taking hold, and Europe is watching closely
articles.summary: A movement that began in outrage has delivered one of Europe’s most remarkable election upsets, showing that change is possible and prompting questions over what comes next
body: In April of last year, dozens of students set off from Serbia, intent on making it to Strasbourg, France on bicycles. The aim of the arduous, 13-day transcontinental journey was simple: to make their voices heard in Europe and beyond.

In their home city of Novi Sad, students had been holding near-daily protests after a deadly roof collapse at the city’s main railway station. As their push for accountability and justice spread across the country, it was met with baton-wielding police, teargas and a political class that branded these young people as traitors.

Their trek to Strasbourg was aimed at casting a spotlight on the deepening erosion of democratic values in their home country. “Serbia needs Europe’s support,” the students explained in an open letter to the French president, Emmanuel Macron, as they arrived in Strasbourg and met with MEPs and officials. “We are not riding toward Europe to flee Serbia. We are riding to bring it back.”

On Sunday, their movement made headlines across the world as the students were catapulted from the streets of Serbia into the halls of power. In a ballot that saw the highest turnout since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992, over 50% of voters backed the students to oust the increasingly authoritarian leader, Aleksandar Vučić, and end his party’s 14 years in power.
It was, as a Guardian editorial noted, “one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history”.

The students’ extraordinary feat came as Europe has been rocked by weeks of protests. From Porto to Paris and Madrid to Milan, analysts have pointed to the common thread that weaves through the diverse protests: a view that the social contract has broken down, leaving younger generations bracing for a future in which they will be worse off than their parents.

The election result in Serbia lays bare the power of these protests to reshape politics, postdoctoral researcher Aleksandar Matković noted this week. Could it be, as WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange once told an interviewer in Belgrade, that Serbia is “a country where the future happens first”?

Matković drew on his involvement inside the student movement to offer a singular window into all that had gone into their win, citing discussions that had stretched as long as six hours as the students laid the groundwork for their entry into politics. “The world should be watching closely: it may be witnessing the start of a very different kind of politics,” he wrote.

Their win sparked joy across Serbia, sending tens of thousands of jubilant revelers on to streets across the country. “It’s very strange that on the very streets where the police beat us, on the streets where we retreated countless times in the face of the gendarmerie, we are now standing here as the victors,” Sara, 24, told the Guardian.
Hours later supporters of the movement appeared again, this time to clean up after a night of raucous celebrations.

The movement now faces a tremendous task – particularly given that it has no hierarchy or leader. For more than a decade, Vučić’s party had transformed the state, tightening its grip on media, stuffing institutions with loyalists to the party and wielding ministries and Serbian institutions as political tools.

The movement won 140 of the 250 seats in parliament, giving a comfortable majority to a slate of candidates who range from academics to athletes, and who were chosen via student assemblies in the lead-up to the election. As one candidate told my colleagues on Monday, the top priority was “the social and psychological detoxification” of the country.

Underpinning the movement is an 11-point plan, which includes ridding the country of corruption, reforming the judiciary and media and improving access to healthcare. “We are neither promising, nor expecting overnight miracles as a result of this victory,” one member of the movement wrote in the Guardian this week. “Rather we hope for something fundamentally radical for Serbia: normal, functioning institutions.”

And while their plans for power take shape, the impact of their bold experiment will certainly be felt far beyond Serbia. The country applied to join the European Union in 2009, but the process has largely stalled in recent years. Now, much like in neighbouring Hungary, the elections have ushered in the possibility of a fresh start along with hope of a democratic resurgence in central Europe.

As EU officials sent their congratulations this week to the students, whose policy platform promises to put the question of future EU membership to a referendum, a note of optimism laced their messages. “We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union,” the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, said on social media.
Marta Kos, the EU’s enlargement commissioner, was more direct. “A new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together,” she wrote on social media.

It was a stunning reversal of fortunes for the students who last year felt they had to cycle more than 1,300km (780 miles) to make their voices heard. Now – after nearly two years of protests that were met with detentions on trumped-up evidence, illegal surveillance, threats and job losses – it seems they might have a chance to fulfil their wish of bringing Europe to Serbia.

articles.title: Israel election: what we know so far
articles.summary: With nearly all votes counted, Netanyahu’s coalition government has lost its majority, but main opponents also fail to gain outright majority; marked gains by Palestinian parties
body: With almost all votes counted, Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government has lost its majority, but his main opponents, an alliance of Jewish Israeli parties unofficially led by Gadi Eisenkot, have also failed to gain an outright majority.

Israeli media report that Netanyahu’s bloc is ahead, with projections he could take 53 seats under the current vote share, but this could change further. The projections put Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc on 48 seats and the Palestinian parties on 19 seats. Sixty-one seats are needed to form a majority to govern in the Knesset.
The remainder of votes to be counted come from absentee ballots, according to Israeli media. We can expect absentee ballots to be counted on Wednesday night, with final results by Thursday.

The Palestinian Israeli parties have received a historically strong vote. The Joint List, a new ticket of several Arab-majority parties, triumphed with at least 12 seats, while Ra’am, the other Islamic party, won seven.

The key question is whether the Eisenkot-led “Change” bloc (consisting of the rightwinger Naftali Bennett’s Together party, the centre-left Yair Golan’s Democrats and the rightwing Yisrael Beiteinu party) will partner with Palestinian Israeli parties or if they will resort to a new election, or even working with Netanyahu.

Netanyahu took the stage at a post-election rally in Jerusalem just after 3am, telling his supporters that official results will show that “Likud is the largest party in Israel”. He told his supporters that the country must “establish a strong, rightwing national government” – adding that a government that relied on the support of Palestinian parties must not be formed.

Eisenkot told cheering supporters in Tel Aviv that the “Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu’s service as Israel’s prime minister … a worthy leader would have accepted the people’s non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics”. In his speech, he also warned Netanyahu not to “use Israel’s security” for political ends, playing on fears that the prime minister could use this period of uncertainty to launch a new attack on Iran.

The Palestinian Israeli vote, which represents about 20% of the population, had long been seen as a decisive factor for who will be able to form government, and the high turnout of this election was driven by the community experiencing increased racism and discrimination under Netanyahu’s government.
This is the most voted-for election in Israel’s political history, with many Israelis flying back into the country to cast their vote, and nearly 80% of IDF soldiers voting.
Donald Trump said his endorsement had helped Netanyahu perform better than polling estimates.

articles.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
articles.summary: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website
body: Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.
Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.
According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.
Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.
Related: The news website that’s keeping press freedom alive in Egypt | Leslie T Chang
Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.
Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after Brazil election loss
articles.summary: Far-right senator and family land in US after crossing from Brazil into Argentina and then flying via Ecuador
body: A private jet carrying the Brazilian far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro has landed in Miami, Florida, where the losing candidate in Sunday’s presidential election runoff left the airport under police escort without speaking to the press.

After losing Sunday’s election to the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Bolsonaro disappeared for more than 24 hours, until Argentina’s migration authorities said he had entered the country by land on Tuesday night.

There, he boarded a Gulfstream IV registered as LV-JQW, which had been parked at Puerto Iguazú airport since the early hours of the previous morning, when the first reports emerged in Argentinian media that he intended to flee on it.

Bolsonaro, the son of the jailed former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, boarded the jet with his wife and two teenage daughters at about 11.30pm, bound for Guayaquil in Ecuador, reportedly to avoid Brazilian airspace. They made a brief stop in Ecuador and continued on to Miami-Opa Locka airport, about 11 miles north of downtown Miami, a private aviation hub catering to corporate executives and wealthy travelers.

Bolsonaro, wearing a black bulletproof vest and looking somber, and his family emerged from the plane into a postcard-perfect sunny South Florida morning at 9:24am. They briefly remained inside the airport before leaving, shielded by black umbrellas, climbing into a dark gray Ford Expedition MAX and speeding away under police escort.

He said nothing before boarding the vehicle and the mood was low-key, without any supporters present to welcome him and only two dozen journalists who were shooed away by two Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents.
He is expected to hold a press conference in the US today or tomorrow.
A senior US state department official told media outlets that visas would be granted to Bolsonaro and his family, and on Tuesday night Donald Trump said he would approve their move to the country.

“They’re fine people. The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Trump said as he returned from a campaign event in Texas. “I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flávio a little bit. I know the father very well.”

Lula called Bolsonaro’s flight “shameful”. “This is what the Bolsonaro family are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as they’ve become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.

Some in the Brazilian government suspected Bolsonaro allies had spent Tuesday privately telling the press he was already on his way to the US to distract from his real plan to go through Argentina. The federal police are facing criticism for failing to prevent him from leaving the country.

There is a gap between the last time he was seen by allies at about 6pm on Monday and the moment he entered Argentina late on Tuesday. It remains unclear how or when he travelled to the border, or where he was during that time.
Footage from a television channel there shows two vans crossing the border checkpoint and then being escorted by airport security officers to the airport.

The Argentinian newspaper Página/12 reported that the aircraft belonged to the businessman Sergio Daniel Mastropietro, who was investigated by local police in one of the biggest scandals of Javier Milei’s administration, involving the alleged payment of bribes linked to the purchase of medicines for people with disabilities.

Bolsonaro is under investigation in at least two criminal cases, one of them examining suspicions that the senator was involved in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.

It was in connection with that case that, shortly after the election result, Brazilian police asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s passport to be retained over concerns he could flee, citing an interview given last Friday by his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro.

Speaking on a podcast in the US, where he is in self-imposed exile and lobbying the Trump administration against Lula, Eduardo said if his brother were to lose the election, he should not concede and should go to the US.

O Globo newspaper reported that the escape had been planned for weeks as a contingency in case he lost, and that Eduardo had been its main organiser, holding talks with US officials about receiving the senator.

Fleeing Brazil has almost become standard practice among Bolsonaro supporters facing criminal charges or convictions in the country: about a dozen politicians or influencers closely aligned with Jair Bolsonaro have done the same in recent years.

The former president himself spent three months in Florida shortly after losing the 2022 election. He later returned to Brazil and, while facing trial over the attempted coup, spent two nights at the Hungarian embassy in Brasília, then run by his ally Viktor Orbán.
While under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years in prison, the patriarch of the Bolsonaro clan used a soldering iron in an attempt to destroy his electronic ankle monitor.

articles.title: Soviet troops invade Hungary – archive, 1956
articles.summary: On 4 November 1956, Russian forces moved into Budapest as part of an offensive against a national uprising that called for democratic reforms and an end to Soviet occupation
body: Before dawn yesterday Soviet armoured forces moved into Budapest and attacked “rebel” strongholds. At 8am the Soviet High Command in Hungary ordered Imre Nagy’s government to surrender by noon “or Budapest will be bombed”. Soviet armoured forces then went into action. Just after 1pm Moscow radio announced: “The Hungarian counter-revolution has been crushed.”

A mid-afternoon Moscow radio bulletin said that negligible groups of insurgents were offering resistance in Budapest but were being crushed. The radio also announced that a new “Revolutionary Workers’ and Peasants’ Government” had been formed under János Kádár, the former “Titoist” who became first secretary of the Communist party at one point in the rebellion.
Related: The Hungarian revolution begins – archive, October 1956

Budapest radio had gone off the air at 8.10am with a woman’s appeal to “help Hungary … help, help, help …” In mid-afternoon a Vienna monitor picked up what was apparently the last rebel-held radio station in Hungary. It broadcast repeated calls for help.

Civilised people of the world. On the watch tower of 1,000-year-old Hungary the last flames begin to go out. Soviet tanks and guns are roaring over Hungarian soil. Our women – mothers and daughters – are sitting in dread. They still have terrible memories of the army’s entry in 1945. Save our souls. This word may be the last from the last Hungarian freedom station. Listen to our call. Help us – not with advice, not with words, but with action, with soldiers and arms.

The last news from Budapest itself reached the British Foreign Office in mid-afternoon. This said that Soviet troops were in control of key points and bridges in the city, although gunfire was still in progress. Other reports said that Mr Nagy, who attempted to restore democracy in the country after the insurrection, was under arrest, together with members of his government.

Mr Nagy – now arrested – had given news of the Soviet attack to the world in a dramatic broadcast over Budapest radio. He spoke in English and then repeated his message in Hungarian. “This is Imre Nagy speaking,” he said. “In the early hours of this morning, Soviet troops started to attack the Hungarian capital with the apparent purpose of overthrowing the democratic government of the Hungarian People’s Republic.” After broadcasting frequent appeals to Russian troops not to fire on peaceful citizens, the radio then went off the air.

Eisenhower appeals to BulganinMr Nagy, before he disappeared, had appealed through the British Legation for immediate intervention by the United Nations. Russia vetoed discussion of Hungary in the Security Council but the General Assembly, where the veto does not rule, voted overwhelmingly for an American resolution calling on the Soviet Union to halt its armed attack on Hungary and withdraw all its forces “without delay.”

President Dwight D Eisenhower sent an urgent message to Marshal Bulganin, the Soviet Premier, asking him to withdraw the Soviet troops. The president expressed “shock and dismay” at the Soviet attack on the Hungarian people and urged that Hungary be given the right to choose its own government.

Sopron, 4 NovemberIn this small town, the most westerly in Hungary, the last minutes of the revolution ran out to the rattle of machine-gun fire, the rumble of Soviet tanks, the screams and tears of women, and the singing of the Hungarian national anthem.

Until 3pm, no Russian troops had entered Sopron, but they were known to be all around it, in the hills and woods. I arrived at Klingenbach, the nearest point in Austria, at three o’clock and decided to go in and have a look for myself. Approaching the Klingenbach I saw streams of Hungarian refugees, walking in little groups along the road, carrying their worldly belongings on their backs, or on oxcarts, handcarts or bicycles.Continue reading.
Related: Political turmoil and street protests: rebellion’s bitter legacy lives on

The “forest fire,” as the prime minister calls it, has not been put out. The flames are rising – and not only in the Middle East. They have spread to eastern Europe. For months or years to come it will be a matter of debate whether Britain’s attack on Egypt sparked Russia’s attack on Hungary. To say the least however, it is possible that British aggression tipped the scales in Soviet planning towards violent action: and British defiance of Assembly resolutions has sapped the strength of the United Nations at a most critical moment. Where Britain has rejected the Assembly’s wishes, Russia (though her crime may be greater) can follow. For the present, Hungary is doomed.

For Hungary and eastern Europe there is tragically little that can be done. Russia can be condemned in the United Nations, but after the past week’s events that will mean little. It remains to be seen whether Russia is turning back entirely to a Stalinist line in foreign policy. Certainly the bankruptcy of its ideology has been displayed to the world in Hungary. If brute force is to be its method in future, we must expect mounting tension also between east and west in Europe.This is an edited extract. Read in full.

Throughout the western countries governments and peoples yesterday protested against the Russians’ suppression of the Hungarian revolt. Even in Poland, still a communist country, a party leader expressed sympathy with the Hungarians.

The official Yugoslav reaction was equivocal. The official news agency, Tanjug, said the use of foreign troops to clear up the internal affairs of a nation was contrary to the principles of Yugoslavia’s foreign policy, “but we cannot avoid the fact that the use of those troops was the result of a negative development in Hungary. Yugoslavs have with great concern followed the strong tendencies of reactionary elements, especially in Budapest – with murders of innocent people, the setting fire to books, and slogans which were smelling of the return to the Horthy era.”

Moscow Radio accused Britain and France of raising the Hungarian question in the United Nations as a “smokescreen for the Anglo-French aggression in the Suez canal zone.” The broadcast went on: “Representatives of certain western powers should be the last ones to pose as defenders of the Hungarian people. It was precisely the long subversive activity of the imperialist powers that inspired and directed the actions of the reactionary forces in Budapest.”
Paris: The French foreign minister, M Pineau, said France regretted that the United Nations had preferred to talk about Egypt rather than support the valiant Hungarian people.

Berlin: The West Berlin radio stations played solemn music in contrast to their usually light Sunday programme. The communist radio of East Berlin continued its normal programme, including dance music. The East German Radio said it had received numerous telephone calls from workers offering help for Hungary or suggesting the creation of an “international brigade to assist the Hungarian workers in the struggle for freedom.”
Copenhagen: About a thousand Danish students demonstrated outside the Russian embassy.

articles.title: Australia must recruit hundreds more to crew Aukus submarines, retired admiral warns
articles.summary: As USS Colorado showcases the program in Perth, Peter Briggs says personnel is just one of the ‘huge issues’ it faces
body: Australia faces an uphill battle to recruit and train enough naval personnel to serve on submarines planned for the future fleet of nuclear-powered vessels under the controversial $368bn Aukus deal, a retired admiral has warned.

As the Virginia-class submarine USS Colorado arrived at HMAS Stirling south of Perth on Tuesday for a month of routine maintenance and to help build Australian expertise, retired admiral Peter Briggs said more people needed to be enrolled in the navy’s submarine program.
Related: We want you! ADF recruitment rates are growing, even as the odds of conflict rise. Why are people signing up?

As part of a $368bn trilateral defence deal, Australia will acquire between three and five Virginia-class, nuclear-powered submarines from the United States to replace its five diesel-electric Collins-class vessels, which are becoming obsolete.
The new submarines are much bigger and require up to 134 crew – almost three times the number needed for the Collins class.
The Royal Australian Navy says it has 230 personnel in various stage of the US nuclear-powered submarine training pipeline.

“Of these, approximately 145 have completed US Naval nuclear power training and are now building experience training on US Navy SSNs [a hull classification for nuclear-powered submarines],” a navy spokesperson said.
“By 2030, we expect to have 400 Royal Australian Navy officers and sailors trained and ready to serve.”
But Briggs urged a more intensive recruitment plan to crew the bigger boats.
Related: Hegseth calls US-built nuclear submarines the ‘apex predator’ of the seas. But are they right for Australia?
“We have got to triple the size of the submarine arm and we’ve got to train them in nuclear skills,” he said.
“You are heading toward needing a submarine arm of 3,000, that’s the hill you have to climb.”
Approximately 850 submariners are qualified to operate Collins-class vessels.
The Virginia-class boats are intended to bridge the transition from the Collins-class fleet to the future SSN-AUKUS submarine, an even bigger design being developed by Australia and the UK.
“The personnel side is a huge issue, but it’s not the only one,” Briggs said.
The former submariner argued that maintaining two different submarine types would add complexity to training, logistics, maintenance and spare-parts arrangements.
The Australian government did not respond to questions about recruitment targets and whether a workforce development program was on track.
Recruitment is further complicated by the need for more than a dozen different trades, from radio and sonar operators to cooks and electricians.

After spending the next month is Perth, the USS Colorado will return to the city’s waters again in late 2027 as part of the Submarine Rotational Force-West program which is designed to help Australia build the skills and infrastructure to operate its own nuclear fleet.
From 2027, the program will see up to four US and one UK nuclear-powered submarine rotate through HMAS Stirling.

Paul Johnson, HMAS Stirling fleet base west commodore, said the USS Colorado maintenance period would be used to “practise and test our procedures across a range of nuclear-related operational scenarios”.
Officials stressed that no radiological material would be transferred during the maintenance period and that nuclear-related exercises would be simulated.
Late last year, Senate estimates heard that US submarines carrying nuclear weapons could rotate through Australian ports despite a non-proliferation commitment.
USS Colorado captain, Justin Reeves, said the US government would not “confirm or deny the presence of nuclear weapons on specific platforms”.
Colorado was built in 2018 and arrived this week carrying conventional weapons, including four torpedoes and four “payload tubes” that can be used to house and launch weapons.

It took two weeks to travel to Perth from Pearl Harbor in Hawaii with 160 men and no women aboard. A sign labelled “Berth Rules”, taped to the wall near the submarine’s entryway, listed “Don’t be stinky” as the crew’s top priority once they reach port.
The demands of living and working in confined spaces for extended periods presents another recruitment challenge for officials.
Sleeping arrangements can involve bunks stacked three high, while “hot racking” allows three sailors to share two beds by rotating their sleeping schedules around watch duties.
In some circumstances, and when accommodation is limited, sailors may sleep in torpedo rooms.
Reeves said the vessel is “built for combat, not for comfort”.
Nuclear submarines don’t need to refuel, meaning their range is effectively infinite. “The limits of its endurance are really food and toilet paper, and that’s several months’ worth,” Reeves said.
“Being nuclear powered is a massive advantage.”

articles.title: King Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summit
articles.summary: Royal tour of Caribbean comes as poll suggests majority support among younger Britons for dialogue on slavery reparations
body: King Charles has confirmed he will discuss the legacy of slavery at a summit with Commonwealth leaders as he begins his Caribbean tour.

The king arrived in the Bahamas on Tuesday to a ceremonial welcome and attended a youth rally at Clifford Park, the site where the country officially gained its independence from British colonial rule in 1973.
His arrival comes as a poll suggested strong support among young people and Labour voters in the UK for a dialogue on slavery reparations.

The poll, conducted by More in Common last week and published by the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, found that 40% of Britons supported a meeting on reparatory justice, while 19% were undecided.

But Repair Campaign elder and former St Vincent and the Grenadines prime minister Ralph Gonsalves pointed to disaggregated data showing that support was considerably higher among younger people, with 60% of those aged 18-24 and 51% of those aged 25-34 backing a meeting on reparatory justice.
The poll also suggested that a majority of all ages who voted Labour (58%) and Liberal Democrat (57%) in the last election favoured a meeting.
The findings come as the UK faces intensifying pressure from Caribbean leaders to apologise for its role in slavery and agree to a structured dialogue on reparations.

“The bulk of the young people under the age of 35 are saying we have to have that conversation. This should prompt him, like the Dutch prime minister, to give a full formal apology,” Gonsalves told the Guardian.

He also urged King Charles to apologise and help establish mechanisms for a dialogue, adding that he was disappointed with the King’s maiden speech in the Bahamas, which he described as “falling far short of what he had said before”.

Charles acknowledged the “appalling atrocity of slavery”, describing it as something “which forever stains our history, when he attended the ceremony marking Barbados’s historic transition to a republic in 2021.

A year later he described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to “deepen my own understanding of slavery’s enduring impact”, in a speech at the opening of a Commonwealth summit hosted by Rwanda.
In his speech in the Bahamas on Tuesday, Charles said: “Some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness.

“It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future.”
He said the leaders at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) would discuss matters relating to the legacy of slavery next week in Antigua.
Charles’s nine-day tour, which includes a solo state visit to Guyana, will culminate in presiding over the Chogm gathering, hosted by Antigua and Barbuda.
But a statement from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee said the king’s comments on Tuesday “fall short of what justice requires”.

“Our culture is not born out of darkness; our culture was born out of agency and out of the will to survive despite the horrors, trauma and degradation. Our culture is a testament to the power of the human spirit, not simply a reaction to the worst examples of it.
“We therefore do not need King Charles to tell us how outstanding our culture is … We need him to speak about his role in the darkness and how he plans to atone for it actively.

“The royal family and the British government were responsible for the darkness. His comments fall short of what justice requires – a full and formal apology – and they do not speak to the steps needed to remedy the wrongs committed in the name of the crown he wears.”

Dr Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, the committee’s chair, told the Guardian that while she appreciated the king’s attempt to “connect with Bahamian culture” in his speech his words felt “like hollow platitudes”.

She added: “I am very proud of my Bahamian people and the beautiful spirit and hospitality that they shared. My critique is not an attempt to rain on their parade. It is because of this pride that I feel we deserve so much more than what was offered.”
Related: King Charles urged ‘as human brother’ to support reparations talks at Caribbean summit
The chair of the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, Prof Hilary Beckles, said what the Caribbean was looking for was “proprietary justice, beginning with remorse”.

Beckles added that when speaking to Caribbean young people the king should “dig deep within his consciousness” and give to them “the empowerment that he would give to his own children” to survive in a rapidly changing world. Anything short of that would be to condone and minimise the legacy of harm and suffering that continues today, he said.
Charles is to travel to Guyana on Thursday where the president, Mohamed Irfaan Ali, recently called for the monarch to take the next step and offer to apologise.
The king follows the guidance of his ministers, and it is understood the government has not advised him to offer an apology or reparations, in keeping with established policy.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will join Charles in Antigua for the gathering of Commonwealth leaders.

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: “At the request of host governments, the king’s programme will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future that are having a transformative effect on the region, as it confronts the challenges of today.

“For his majesty, this tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past. This will therefore also be reflected in differing ways and words during the tour, as you would expect.”
Announcing the poll results, Repair Campaign founder Denis O’Brien called for a “time-lined commitment to holding talks with Caribbean states”.

“To date, there have been too many unsubstantiated expressions of regret and sorrow about Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, coupled with empty promises – including at the last Chogm in Samoa – that some sort of dialogue would begin,” he said.
Additional reporting by Press Association

articles.title: Wednesday briefing: We asked you - what do you want from the Burnham government’s first budget?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: First Edition readers and people struggling with the cost of living tell us what the government could do to improve their lives
body: Good morning. Don’t expect anything radical. This, the Treasury has been at pains to tell us, will be a very “low-key” budget. After weeks of speculation from journalists, a flurry of press releases from thinktanks, and a photoshoot with an obligatory red box, the chancellor, John Healey, will announce the details of the Burnham government’s first budget in the Commons today at 12:30pm.

Healey has been selling this as a series of measures designed to relieve pressure on low- and middle-income households under the mangled tagline of “breathing space for today, fresh hope for the future”. Many of the proposals have already been briefed, and their modesty is a sign of the constraints – both real and self-imposed – that his government faces. He has rejected calls to raise capital gains tax or lower the mansion tax and has promised to stick to Labour’s fiscal rules, while the Iran war has increased the cost of borrowing and eroded his spending power.

Voters might be hoping for something transformative from a government that risks presiding over the worst parliament for living standards on record. That’s the impression I got from First Edition readers and people struggling with the cost of living, who I spoke to for this morning’s newsletter about what they’d like to see from today’s budget. First, here are the headlines.

Israeli elections | Israel could be in for weeks of political haggling after exit polls and partial official results showed neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor the opposition bloc led by former general Gadi Eisenkot had won enough seats to form a government.

Energy | The government’s plan to fund a multibillion-pound nuclear plant at the Sizewell site in Suffolk represents a “terrible deal” for the UK taxpayer over the rest of the century, according to the government’s spending watchdog.

Middle East | A multipronged peace deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within four days of sanctions being lifted and for the Houthis to withdraw substantial forces inside Yemen are at the heart of Gulf states’ plans to avert what they regard as a disastrous renewal of war between Iran and the US.

UK news | A 78-year-old volunteer has claimed a Reform UK councillor accused her of “facilitating the invasion” and being akin to a Nazi collaborator during the second world war because she has helped asylum seekers learn English.

Brazil | The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

There was some detectable grumbling earlier this week over the lack of information about this budget compared with those of Rachel Reeves, and Healey has made much of the “military-style protocols” that have allegedly stopped the Treasury’s secrets from leaking out. But it seems more likely that there hasn’t been much to leak. “It’s going to be a far smaller budget than last year,” Kiran Stacey, the Guardian’s policy editor, told me on Monday. “It’s not going to be ending 40 years of neoliberalism.”
